cues.text: A Contested Election
Born around 304, probably in Rome, to a family that served the church of the martyr St. Lawrence, Damasus was elected pope in October 366 by a large majority.
A faction of zealous supporters of his predecessor's rival, however, refused to accept the result.
They irregularly consecrated the deacon Ursinus as a rival claimant, creating a schism that led to genuine violence and bloodshed in Rome's streets before Damasus's position was secured.
Defender of Nicene Orthodoxy
Once firmly established, Damasus vigorously defended Nicene orthodoxy against the lingering heresies of Arianism, Macedonianism, and Apollinarianism.
He formally excommunicated the Arian bishop Auxentius of Milan at a Roman synod around 369–370.
He convened further councils that clarified and reaffirmed the Church's teaching on the Trinity and the Holy Spirit.
Commissioning the Vulgate
Damasus's most consequential act may have been his commission to his brilliant secretary, St. Jerome , to revise the confused and inconsistent Old Latin translations of the Gospels.
These were then in use across the Western Church, beginning the project that would eventually grow into Jerome's complete Latin Vulgate, the Bible of the West for the next fifteen centuries.
Damasus also introduced Latin as the liturgical language of the Roman Mass in place of Greek during his pontificate.
Poet of the Martyrs
Damasus is remembered with particular affection for his deep personal devotion to Rome's early martyrs.
He composed dozens of elegant verse epitaphs—the celebrated 'Damasan tituli'—to mark and honor their tombs throughout the catacombs.
His friend Furius Dionysius Filocalus inscribed them in a distinctive lettering.

He personally restored and drained sections of the catacombs to protect the martyrs' remains from water damage, work that modern archaeology, particularly the labors of Giovanni Battista De Rossi, has done much to recover and appreciate.
Legacy

Damasus's twin achievements — commissioning the Vulgate and lovingly restoring the physical memory of Rome's martyrs — mark him as a pivotal bridge between the age of persecution and the flourishing of Latin Christian culture that followed.
He is honored today as the patron saint of archaeologists, in recognition of his own careful, reverent excavation and preservation of the early Church's most sacred sites.
